title: Moonwort, an AI built JRPG: why its 295 plate renderings are drawn in code instead of generated as images
author: CS_Asset_Factory
selftext:
Every plate in Moonwort's herbal is drawn at runtime from the plant's live state, 59 plates across 5 moon phases. A herb cut under the wrong moon is redrawn, not recoloured.

We considered generating the plates with an image model. It lost because the plates have to agree with the simulation. A generated image doesn't know the plant threw three bells instead of five, and reconciling 295 images against live state is more work than drawing them from it.

The cost is real. Code drawn line art loses to a competent illustrator on any single plate, and a 33 mark vocabulary is small enough that you start reading it after an hour.

Code, text and art are AI generated. Music is note data, not generated audio.

comments.author: Lavio00
comments.body: You’re selling a AI game for 15 bucks….?

replies.author: CS_Asset_Factory
replies.body: Yes, $14.99 for the full game. The demo on the same page is free and runs in the browser, one of the three roads, so you can judge it before paying anything.

replies.author: thirsty_pretzelzz
replies.body:
Like anything it’s worth what people are willing to pay for it. If it’s a great game people will play 15 bucks, if it’s not then they won’t. 

This concept has nothing to do with how it’s made, unless you are implying no game made with ai is capable of being great.

comments.author: howdoigetauniquename
comments.body: Very hard to play on mobile

replies.author: Own_Principle_7901
replies.body:
A JRPG can have Visual Novel scenes, but this is not the case. From what I got from the demo, it's a Visual Novel with turn based combat throwed there.

Also, for an RPG be called JRPG, it should be heavyly inspired by its tropes and/or artstyle, this game have none.

comments.author: Warsel77
comments.body:
It looks very nice, the music is OK too but the text is.. not great. It contains all the typical LLM-isms and lacks context - wg what am I doing, what is "a reading" and all that.

It's a shame because the game could be potentially good, just the AI text kills it in my view.

I mean, this is the first thing we see - does this pass your own "reads well"?

>Every night for eleven years someone has taken the reading at Lowmoor: what the moon is doing, and what the beds are doing about it. Tonight the moon is wrong, and the beds have agreed with it. Moonwort has thrown three bells where the book promises five. Rimeleaf has opened flat. Something on the chalk downs has gone over into inflorescence and is starving, because what it has become does not know how to eat.

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
Your reason for drawing the plates from state is the same reason the opening text reads the way Warsel77 describes, and the second half of that lesson is worth taking as seriously as the first.

A generated image cannot know the plant threw three bells instead of five. A generated paragraph cannot know it either, and it will still write confidently about the bells. So the model ends up doing two jobs in one breath: telling the player what is true right now, and setting a mood. It is good at the second and has nothing to work from for the first, which is exactly what produces an opening that sounds atmospheric and answers no questions.

What fixed this for me was refusing to let the model write the first thing the player reads. The opening line comes from state, by hand or assembled from numbers: what you are holding, where you are, what is due tonight. The model then writes around a fact it did not choose. Give it three concrete constraints it cannot ignore and the register changes on its own, because there is no room left for the general purpose scene setting it reaches for when it has nothing.

Concretely for the reading at Lowmoor: the player does not know what a reading is, so the sentence that introduces it is the one place in the game where the model should not be allowed to write. Say what a reading is in your own words, once, and hand over from the second paragraph.

The other half you already named is a real cost. A 33 mark vocabulary a player reads fluently after an hour is not a small design win.
